analysis.one_liner: Expiring every new federal regulation after one year unless Congress votes to keep it.
analysis.headline: The bill was introduced in November 2017, referred to two House committees, sent to a subcommittee, and never received a hearing or vote before the 115th Congress ended in January 2019.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have ended every new federal rule one year after it is finalized unless Congress passed a law specifically extending it. Because Congress passes legislation for individual rules only rarely, most new regulations — from food safety to workplace protections to air quality standards — would simply expire. Federal agencies write the detailed rules that carry out laws Congress passes; this bill would have made that rulemaking temporary by default, with Congress required to affirmatively save each rule it liked.
analysis.who_benefits: Businesses subject to new federal regulation. Any rule that raises their costs — on emissions, product safety, financial practices, wages, or consumer disclosures — would lapse within a year unless both chambers of Congress voted to keep it. Since Congress rarely legislates on individual rules, companies could expect most new restrictions to disappear.

how_it_helps.text: Every rule finalized after enactment would automatically expire one year later, giving regulated firms a default outcome of no new regulation rather than a permanent new rule.
A rule could survive only if Congress enacted a joint resolution to continue it, putting the burden of saving protections on Congress rather than on industry to remove them.

analysis.who_pays: Everyone who depends on federal rules for protection: workers relying on workplace safety standards, consumers relying on product and financial rules, and communities relying on clean-air and clean-water rules. Under the bill's design, nearly all new protections would lapse unless Congress affirmatively saved them, which it almost never does for individual rules.
analysis.who_pays_short: Workers, consumers, and communities protected by rules

drawbacks.text: Federal agencies finalize thousands of rules each year to carry out laws Congress has already passed; requiring a joint resolution to keep each one would make routine, congressionally mandated protections temporary by default.

The automatic one-year expiration would apply to all new rules with no screening for importance, so protections on health, safety, wages, and the environment would end unless Congress acted for each rule individually.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit runs to regulated businesses: reduced and time-limited compliance costs. The cost is paid broadly by the public, which would lose most new federal protections by default, since Congress does not typically pass individual resolutions to save rules. The bill was not debated in committee or on the floor, so no amended version was ever considered.

outcome.mechanism: The bill sat in two House committees and a subcommittee without a hearing or vote, and expired when the 115th Congress ended on January 3, 2019.

narrative.text: Representative Trent Kelly introduced the bill on November 7, 2017, with one Republican cosponsor.
It was referred to the House Oversight and Government Reform Committee and the House Judiciary Committee on the day it was introduced.
On December 13, 2017, the Judiciary portion was referred to its Subcommittee on Regulatory Reform, Commercial and Antitrust Law.
No further action was recorded before the 115th Congress ended on January 3, 2019, leaving the bill dead without any committee vote or floor vote.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: The public that relies on federal regulatory protections is better off, because no new rule would face automatic expiration; the businesses that stood to benefit from the sunset never gained anything.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: People who rely on federal regulations

for.name: Rep. Trent Kelly
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and recruited one cosponsor.

against.name: Bob Goodlatte
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled the bill for committee action after its referral to the Judiciary Committee.

against.role: Chair, House Oversight and Government Reform Committee
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled the bill for committee action after its referral to the Oversight Committee.

sides.party_line_note: The bill was sponsored by a Republican and cosponsored by one Republican, with no Democratic support recorded, and no votes were ever held on it.

industries.industry: Regulated businesses across the economy (manufacturers, energy producers, financial firms, employers)
industries.note: The bill would make every new federal rule lapse within a year unless Congress saved it, giving regulated firms a default of no new restrictions. That relief comes directly at the expense of the protections those rules provide to workers, consumers, and communities.
